results.name: trial_index_drift
results.description: Pearson correlation between trial_index and the yes response; the model has no time-on-task term so predicts ~0, and an observed value away from null_mean means people drift toward more (positive) or fewer (negative) yeses over the session.

results.name: parity_match_effect
results.description: Among sets of 2+ examples that all share a parity, yes rate for same-parity targets minus yes rate for opposite-parity targets; observed above null_mean means people weight parity more than the model, below means the model overweights the even/odd rules.
results.code:
# name: parity_match_effect
# description: Among sets of 2+ examples that all share a parity, yes rate for same-parity targets minus yes rate for opposite-parity targets; observed above null_mean means people weight parity more than the model, below means the model overweights the even/odd rules.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    n = s.notna().sum(axis=1)
    odd = (s % 2).sum(axis=1)
    all_odd = odd == n
    all_even = odd == 0
    m = (n >= 2) & (all_odd | all_even)
    t_odd = df["target"].astype(int) % 2 == 1
    same = m & (t_odd == all_odd)
    diff = m & (t_odd != all_odd)
    if same.sum() == 0 or diff.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df.loc[same, "rating"].mean() - df.loc[diff, "rating"].mean())

results.name: cell_disagreement
results.description: Mean over (set, target) cells of p_hat*(1-p_hat), where p_hat is the cell's yes rate; observed below null_mean means humans agree more (more extreme, all-or-none generalization) than the model's graded posterior predicts, above means humans are more split.

results.name: far_shared_last_digit_effect
results.description: Among targets more than 10 from every example, yes rate when the target shares its final digit with at least one example minus yes rate when it shares none; observed above null_mean means people generalize on partial digit similarity that the model (which only uses all-examples digit rules) under-produces.
results.code:
# name: far_shared_last_digit_effect
# description: Among targets more than 10 from every example, yes rate when the target shares its final digit with at least one example minus yes rate when it shares none; observed above null_mean means people generalize on partial digit similarity that the model (which only uses all-examples digit rules) under-produces.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(s - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    share = np.nansum((s % 10) == (t[:, None] % 10), axis=1) > 0
    far = d > 10
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    a = far & share; b = far & ~share
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: distance_gradient_slope
results.description: OLS slope of yes on log(1 + distance from target to its nearest example), after subtracting each set's mean yes rate; more negative observed than null_mean means human generalization falls off with numeric distance more steeply than the model predicts, less negative means flatter.
results.code:
# name: distance_gradient_slope
# description: OLS slope of yes on log(1 + distance from target to its nearest example), after subtracting each set's mean yes rate; more negative observed than null_mean means human generalization falls off with numeric distance more steeply than the model predicts, less negative means flatter.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()[:, None].astype(float)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(s - t), axis=1)
    x = np.log1p(d)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    g = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    y = y - pd.Series(y).groupby(g.to_numpy()).transform("mean").to_numpy()
    x = x - pd.Series(x).groupby(g.to_numpy()).transform("mean").to_numpy()
    v = (x * x).sum()
    if v == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float((x * y).sum() / v)

results.name: last_vs_first_example_proximity
results.description: Among multi-example sets, yes rate for targets within 5 of the last-shown example (and farther than 5 from the first) minus yes rate for targets within 5 of the first-shown example (and farther than 5 from the last); the model is order-invariant (null ~0), so observed above null_mean means a recency advantage, below a primacy advantage.
results.code:
# name: last_vs_first_example_proximity
# description: Among multi-example sets, yes rate for targets within 5 of the last-shown example (and farther than 5 from the first) minus yes rate for targets within 5 of the first-shown example (and farther than 5 from the last); the model is order-invariant (null ~0), so observed above null_mean means a recency advantage, below a primacy advantage.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    n = s.notna().sum(axis=1).to_numpy()
    arr = s.to_numpy(dtype=float)
    first = arr[:, 0]
    last = arr[np.arange(len(arr)), np.maximum(n - 1, 0)]
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    df_ = np.abs(t - first); dl = np.abs(t - last)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    a = (n >= 2) & (dl <= 5) & (df_ > 5)
    b = (n >= 2) & (df_ <= 5) & (dl > 5)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: outside_hull_near_yes
results.description: Yes rate for targets lying outside [min, max] of a multi-example set but within 10 of that range (and not in the set); observed above null_mean means people extend similarity-based generalization beyond the examples' range more than the model, below means less.
results.code:
# name: outside_hull_near_yes
# description: Yes rate for targets lying outside [min, max] of a multi-example set but within 10 of that range (and not in the set); observed above null_mean means people extend similarity-based generalization beyond the examples' range more than the model, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric)
    n = s.notna().sum(axis=1)
    lo = s.min(axis=1); hi = s.max(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    gap = np.maximum(lo - t, t - hi)
    m = (n >= 2) & (gap > 0) & (gap <= 10)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df.loc[m, "rating"].mean())

results.name: singleton_set_yes_rate
results.description: Overall yes rate on trials whose set has a single example; observed above null_mean means people generalize more broadly from one example than the model's size-principle posterior, below means more narrowly.
